summary: Console and DNS-mandate headlines dominate AI infrastructure talk, small models keep proving local-first is viable, and open hardware plus a Japanese Mars-moon launch round out the day.

sections.title: AI
sections.summary: A Switch 2 software jailbreak, a DNS resolver walking away from a French court order, agent-safety tooling, and two honest small-model releases.

stories.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
stories.summary: A software-only, tethered jailbreak (ns2jb) targets firmware 23.0.1 by chaining a 32-bit integer overflow in the backward-compatible SmileBASIC interpreter into a path-normalization overflow in the `fs` sysmodule, yielding arbitrary native code without a modchip. The write-up doubles as a candid log of using LLM agents (Codex) for vulnerability research on real hardware, including a JetKVM rig that let the agent drive and observe the console. Nintendo has since pulled SmileBASIC 4 from the eShop; the exploit is non-persistent and vanishes on reboot.

stories.title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France
stories.summary: Quad9 announced it will stop serving France on Nov 24 after a Paris court ruled against it in a beIN Sports piracy-blocking case, shrinking the sought €580k/day penalty to €1,000/day but leaving ~20 other pending cases that the nonprofit says it cannot survive. The principle at stake is that a recursive DNS resolver shouldn't be conscripted into per-jurisdiction content blocking it has no technical way to scope reliably. Worth reading alongside Quad9's own statement for how neutral infrastructure responds when a court tries to turn it into a content gate.

stories.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
stories.summary: A 360M fine-tune of Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B predicts terminal screens one keypress at a time, trained on ~2B tokens of synthetic Docker sessions with DAgger-style self-correction, and runs in-browser via WebGPU (parallel row decoding brings full-screen redraws from ~12s down to under 1s). The author is refreshingly upfront that it's a weak world model — memory across sessions is the hard part — but it's a nice demonstration of small models learning a constrained, structured environment. A fun and technically detailed read for anyone thinking about tiny local models.

stories.title: What's getting pwned right now
stories.summary: A live feed tracking what's actively being exploited in the wild, complementing CVE databases with the more practical question of what's actually being hit today. Useful as a quick daily-or-weekly check for anyone running internet-exposed services. Treat it as a triage dashboard, not a substitute for your own patching process.

stories.title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
stories.summary: NVIDIA's OpenShell (Apache-2.0) provides a policy-governed sandbox for autonomous agents: a declarative YAML policy controls what each agent may touch, enforced via kernel instrumentation (eBPF-based) and formal verification to check policy changes before they apply, with credentials injected as named providers rather than exposed to the agent. Interesting as a pattern for anyone building multi-agent systems that need real file/network/credential access without handing over the whole machine. Docs are early; worth watching how the isolation and policy layers mature.

stories.title: php2shell: PHP session.upload_progress RCE (CVE-2026-109618/109619)
stories.summary: A research PoC repo documents pre-auth RCE chains via PHP's session.upload_progress feature (CVE-2026-109618/109619) with five distinct exploitation paths and ready-to-use Suricata/Sigma/ModSecurity detection rules. Multiple independent PoCs appeared within a day, and OpenAI published a companion checker script. If you run PHP anywhere user-facing, this is worth patching/inspecting against the published chains today rather than waiting for vendor advisories to settle.

stories.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
stories.summary: Anthropic describes work pairing LLM agents with formal proof assistants to verify software properties at a scale that was previously impractical for humans to grind through alone. The framing — LLMs as drafters for machine-checked proofs rather than as the oracle of correctness — is the genuinely interesting part, since it keeps the trust boundary on the verifier, not the model. Worth a read if you care about how AI-assisted engineering might actually raise the correctness floor rather than just output volume.

stories.title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
stories.summary: Investigates how coding agents can pick between coarse 'macro' skills and finer 'micro' ones at runtime, plus how to recover when an agent falls back from a high-level plan to step-by-step execution. Directly relevant to anyone building agent harnesses with skill libraries. Treat as preprint; the title suggests a concrete mechanism but the abstract doesn't commit to numbers.

stories.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
stories.summary: A short, provocative title attacking two of the most load-bearing primitives in modern ML — softmax and cross-entropy — which is inherently interesting because any real fix would ripple through training and inference for essentially every model. Given the scope of the claim, read the paper carefully and look for independent reproduction before taking it as a recipe.

stories.title: Laya-Arabic: a 322M guardrail/typed-decision model for Egyptian Arabic
stories.summary: A 322M-parameter classifier (mmBERT-base encoder + 2-layer decision head) for Arabic-language guardrails and typed decisions — 12-way safety classification, intent routing, prompt-injection detection — with a genuinely detailed model card including held-out F1, per-class breakdown, over-refusal/miss rates, and explicit caveats about what 'zero-shot' means here. Runs comfortably on CPU. One of the better-documented small models released this week.

stories.title: Mavi-1.5B: a Turkish municipal-services chatbot fine-tune with published evals
stories.summary: A Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct QLoRA fine-tune for a fictional Turkish municipality's citizen assistant, with the full training recipe (419 synthetic Gemini-generated conversations, 3 epochs), a before/after eval table against the base model, and — unusually — a published test-question file including cases the model gets wrong (e.g. it refuses water-billing questions it was never trained on). GGUF is provided so it runs on modest hardware. A good example of honest small-model evaluation, including the failures.

sections.title: Electronics
sections.summary: Measurement, tooling, and one classic chip teardown — all reproducible with open files.

stories.title: An Open Source Linear Capacitive Encoder
stories.summary: A 40-micron-resolution linear capacitive encoder built from scratch: a PCB with eight transmitter electrodes and one receiver, read out by an STM32, with schematics and code on GitHub. Same principle as the scales inside cheap digital calipers, but as an open project you can adapt for CNC or metrology use. Files are linked, so this is a real build reference rather than a teaser.

stories.title: KiCad… In The Browser?
stories.summary: ZiroEDA is a TypeScript port of KiCad 10's C++ source that runs the schematic editor, PCB editor, and interactive router entirely in a browser tab — no install, and projects are end-to-end encrypted. Zone fills reportedly match kicad-cli output vertex-for-vertex, which is a strong compatibility signal even though some dialogs are still missing. Source is on GitHub if you'd rather self-host or inspect the port.

stories.title: Floating-Point Addition and Subtraction on Intel's 8087
stories.summary: Ken Shirriff continues his 8087 reverse-engineering series, walking through how the 1980 math coprocessor implements floating-point addition and subtraction in microcode, including the shifter circuitry that dominates the die. A genuinely instructive read on how FPU hardware predates modern IEEE-754 assumptions. Best paired with the earlier posts in the same series for the full picture.

stories.title: CircuitPython 11.0.0-alpha.2 released (ESP32-S31 support lands)
stories.summary: Second alpha of the 11.0.0 series adds `storage.map_file` (read files directly from memory-mapped flash), USB-host audio input for microphones, RGBMatrix ABC row addressing, faster `displayio`, and — new in this release — Espressif ESP32-S31 support. Incompatibility notes worth checking before upgrading: three ports (broadcom, litex, renode) are gone, and Espressif processor UID ordering changed. Alpha quality; not for production boards yet.

stories.title: Building a super-affordable automated PCB inspection system
stories.summary: A six-station turntable PCB inspection rig built from an Arduino UNO Q, a webcam, a servo, and an LED, running YOLO vision models via Edge Impulse to catch missing parts and defects. The whole structure is 3D-printable and the build cost is deliberately low — an interesting reference for anyone doing small-batch PCBA quality control without industrial AOI equipment. Hardware list and code are linked in the post.

stories.title: NASA Batteries Survive Extreme Cold and Heat
stories.summary: An overview of NASA's work on battery electrolytes that keep functioning across extreme temperature swings — relevant to anyone designing for the lunar south pole, Mars rovers, or terrestrial cold-chain/automotive use. The piece focuses on solid-state and electrolyte chemistry rather than a specific build, so it's background reading rather than a how-to, but the temperature ranges and chemistry trade-offs are concretely reported.

sections.title: Interesting News
sections.summary: A mission to bring back a piece of Mars's moon, a gender effect in bird fear responses, a 178-year-old space-weather mystery re-dated, and other verified oddities.

stories.title: JAXA's MMX lifts off to bring back a sample from Mars's moon Phobos
stories.summary: Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched on an H3 rocket from Tanegashima on Oct 19, headed for a first-ever landing on Phobos and a sample return to Earth. Phobos's origin (captured asteroid vs. impact debris from a Mars collision) is still unresolved, and a pristine Phobos sample would settle a lot of that argument. ESA is a partner on the mission's science payload, so its coverage is a good primary source.

stories.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men — and nobody knows why
stories.summary: A study across five European countries and 37 species found urban birds consistently allowed men to get about a metre closer than women before fleeing — an effect that held even when observers were height-, gait-, and clothing-matched, and one that persisted across every country sampled. The authors ran controlled observer-pair experiments to rule out the obvious confounds and still can't explain the mechanism, which is what makes it genuinely interesting rather than just a fun headline. A good example of a robust, reproducible effect with no current explanation.

stories.title: A train delayed by a solar storm — but something didn't add up
stories.byline: ScienceDaily; RMIT University; AGU Space Weather
stories.summary: The famous 1841 'solar storm delayed a train' anecdote — long cited as the first recorded instance of space weather disrupting technology — turns out to be misdated. A re-examination combining railway timetables, newspaper records, and digitized geomagnetic data puts the real event on 18 October 1848, with the Exeter-to-Starcross line not yet existing in 1841 as the tell. The 1847 Midland Railway telegraph disturbance now takes the 'first recorded impact' slot. A neat piece of historical forensics on the earliest overlap between solar activity and human infrastructure.

stories.title: Oxford scientists capture virus-like particles assembling themselves, step by step
stories.summary: Researchers used a mass-photometry technique to watch individual 60-subunit virus-like particles assemble one protein at a time, showing that a simple 'join-and-leave' trial-and-error process reliably reaches the correct closed structure without any template or machinery — the first stable intermediate is a closed 'face' that locks in place and then accelerates the rest of the assembly. The work has direct implications for antiviral strategies and for engineering artificial virus-like particles for vaccines. Published in Nature; the paper link in the article has the full method.

stories.title: TIL: the Aberfan disaster — 60 years on
stories.summary: Exactly 60 years ago today, a colliery spoil tip above the Welsh village of Aberfan slid as a slurry after heavy rain and buried Pantglas Junior School, killing 116 children and 28 adults. The subsequent tribunal found the National Coal Board entirely responsible — the tip had been built over natural springs — and the disaster led directly to the Mines and Quarries (Tips) Act 1966. A somber anniversary worth knowing; the Wikipedia article and the tribunal report are the authoritative references.

stories.title: Honeybees are bullying other pollinators out of flowers
stories.summary: Two years of field observation near Cambridge documented honeybees actively chasing, shoving, and displacing wild bees and hoverflies at flowers — not just outcompeting them by arriving first. On bramble, doubling honeybee density cut bumblebee abundance by 14%; honeybees physically won 20% of contests they initiated, and other pollinators actively avoided them in a quarter to a third of observed interactions. Published in Ecological Entomology; relevant to anyone managing apiaries near wild pollinator habitat.
